unit_name: Conflict and Tension: East and West, 1945-1972
spec_section_focus: Wider world depth study, origins through transformation of the Cold War

teaching_brief.narrative_arc: Lessons walk in chronological order from the wartime alliance breaking down at Yalta and Potsdam (1945), through the consolidation of two armed camps in Europe (Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, Cominform, Berlin Blockade, NATO), into the global widening of the conflict via Asia and the arms and space races, then into the three flashpoint crises (Hungary 1956, U2/Paris Summit, Berlin Wall 1961, Cuba 1962, Czechoslovakia 1968), and finally into the easing represented by Détente, SALT 1 and Nixon-Brezhnev diplomacy. Every lesson re-asks why the Cold War proved so hard to resolve, so that the unit closes with students able to weigh continuity (mistrust, ideology, nuclear weapons) against change (mutual exhaustion, leadership shifts, costs of empire) by 1972.
second_order_concept_focus: Cause: students must distinguish underlying ideological causes (capitalism vs communism, security fears) from triggering events (Truman Doctrine speech, Hungarian protests, U2 shoot-down, missile photographs over Cuba).
Consequence: events at the same site recur (Berlin 1948, 1961) so consequence questions test whether students can track shifting outcomes from the same flashpoint.

Change and continuity: 1945-1949 is rapid change, 1949-1962 is escalation with stable bipolar structure, 1962-1972 is grudging change toward managed coexistence; students struggle to articulate change without flattening continuity.

Significance: examiner reports flag that students judge significance by how dramatic an event was at the time and miss its longer-run impact (Cuba's hotline, Helsinki's human rights clauses, Berlin Wall's stabilising effect on East Germany).

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students arrive with a single-cause explanation, usually 'Stalin started it' or 'America started it', and treat the orthodox or revisionist case as settled fact rather than as a historical interpretation built on partial evidence.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner report commentary on Paper 1 Section B Option C narrative-account questions; Cambridge Core review essays on Cold War origins

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students conflate the 1948-49 Berlin Blockade and Airlift with the 1961 Berlin Wall, blurring two separate crises with different actors, methods and outcomes (Stalin starves the city out vs Khrushchev seals the city in).
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: AQA examiner-style commentary in Cold War teaching guidance on Paper 1 Section B Option C

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students describe the crisis as a clean victory for Kennedy in which Khrushchev backed down, missing the secret deal to withdraw US Jupiter missiles from Turkey and the role of back-channel communication in averting nuclear war.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: History Today archive features on the Cuban Missile Crisis 30 years on and View from Havana

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.topic: Détente and the end of the Cold War
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students assume that because the unit ends in 1972 with Détente and SALT 1, the Cold War effectively ended in the early 1970s, missing that Détente was a specific managed coexistence within a continuing rivalry that intensified again in the late 1970s and 1980s.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: History Today archive on the Soviet-American arms race and SALT; Cambridge History of the Cold War overview chapters

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students believe the West actively supported the Hungarian uprising and was caught off-guard when the Soviets crushed it, when in reality Suez tied down Britain and France, the US chose not to risk war, and the rhetoric of liberation never translated into intervention.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: National Archives Cold War on File materials on Hungary 1956 and Eisenhower-era statements

common_misconceptions_unit_specific.topic: Prague Spring and the Brezhnev Doctrine
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.misconception: Students describe Dubcek's reforms as an attempt to leave the Warsaw Pact, when in fact 'socialism with a human face' was a reform within the bloc, which is precisely why the Brezhnev Doctrine was framed as protecting socialism from internal deviation.
common_misconceptions_unit_specific.source: History Today archive features on Prague's Spring and Why the Prague Spring was Doomed to Failure

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Source-utility responses on this option are strongest when students integrate the source's content, the provenance of its author or government and their own contextual knowledge of bipolar tensions in the relevant year, rather than simply labelling the source 'biased' because it is American or Soviet.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment for Paper 1 Section B and principal examiner report guidance on source-utility questions

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Narrative-account questions reward students who chain events with explicit causal connectives ('this provoked', 'this in turn forced', 'because of this fear') rather than listing dates and incidents in sequence.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA principal examiner report commentary on Paper 1 Section B narrative-account questions

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Top-band answers on the 16-mark source-based essay reach a substantiated overall judgement on the proposition (for example, 'how far Cuba was the most dangerous moment of the Cold War'), weighing it against at least one alternative event in the same period.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.1 and principal examiner commentary on Paper 1 Section B

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Highest-band responses on origins questions show awareness that historians disagree about who was responsible for the Cold War, without needing to name schools of thought; students who write as though there is one settled answer cap themselves below the top band.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: Cambridge Core review essays on Cold War historiography and AQA narrative-account commentary on origins questions

pedagogical_approach: Front-load second-order vocabulary (cause, consequence, significance, change, continuity) in Lesson 1 so students can deploy it in every later lesson — aligns with EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools.

Model expert thinking explicitly on the first source-utility question (Lesson 3) by walking through how to weigh content vs provenance vs contextual knowledge — aligns with EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning.
Use comparative judgement on flashpoints (Berlin 1948 vs Berlin 1961 vs Cuba 1962) because Cambridge Assessment research flags comparative judgement as the hardest GCSE history skill.

Schedule retrieval practice on chronology (1945, 1947, 1948-49, 1950, 1953, 1956, 1957, 1961, 1962, 1968, 1972) every two or three lessons, since narrative-account answers collapse without secure sequencing.

Build interpretation literacy slowly: Lessons 1-4 introduce the language of disagreement (Stalin's view, Truman's view), Lessons 5-10 contrast official sources with later analysis, and Lessons 11-14 invite students to weigh judgement on key turning points.
teaching_brief.research_step_summary: Whitelisted research sources consulted for this unit included AQA's specification page and assessment-resources index for History 8145 Paper 1 Section B Option C, History Today archive features on the Berlin Crises, the Cuban Missile Crisis and Prague's Spring, and the National Archives Cold War on File collection covering Yalta, Potsdam, Berlin Blockade, Marshall Plan, Hungary 1956 and Czechoslovakia 1968. Cambridge Core articles on Cold War historiography were used only to flag the orthodox-revisionist-postrevisionist debate at examiner-signal level, not as named scholars in lesson content. Save My Exams, PMT, MME, Revision World, Primrose Kitten, Study Mind and past-paper PDFs were excluded.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Joseph Stalin
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: Soviet leader at Yalta and Potsdam, architect of the Iron Curtain, Cominform and the Berlin Blockade until his death in 1953.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Winston Churchill
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: British Prime Minister at Yalta, replaced mid-Potsdam, later named the Iron Curtain in his 1946 Fulton speech.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Clement Attlee
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: Took over from Churchill mid-Potsdam, set the British line on a divided Germany and on Marshall aid in early Cold War.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: US President at Yalta, sought to bring Stalin into a postwar UN-led order, died before Potsdam.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Harry S. Truman
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: US President at Potsdam, authorised the atom bomb, gave his name to the Truman Doctrine of containment.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: George C. Marshall
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: US Secretary of State whose 1947 plan tied European recovery to American economic leadership.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Nikita Khrushchev
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: Soviet leader during the Thaw, U2 Crisis, Berlin Wall and Cuban Missile Crisis; his secret-speech reforms triggered Hungary 1956.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Imre Nagy
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: Hungarian reformist leader in 1956 whose attempt to leave the Warsaw Pact triggered Soviet invasion and his execution.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: John F. Kennedy
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: US President during the Berlin Wall crisis and Cuban Missile Crisis, defined the standoff at the Vienna summit and at Checkpoint Charlie.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Fidel Castro
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: Cuban revolutionary leader whose alignment with the USSR after 1959 set up the Bay of Pigs and the missile crisis.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Alexander Dubcek
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: Czechoslovak leader of the Prague Spring's 'socialism with a human face' reforms, removed after the 1968 invasion.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Leonid Brezhnev
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: Soviet leader who issued the Brezhnev Doctrine after Czechoslovakia, then negotiated Détente and SALT 1 with Nixon.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Richard Nixon
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: US President whose visit to Moscow in 1972 produced SALT 1 and gave Détente its public face.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Mao Tse-tung
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: Chinese Communist leader whose 1949 victory shifted the global balance and prompted US fears of falling dominoes in Asia.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: NATO and the Warsaw Pact
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: The two opposing military alliances (1949 and 1955) that institutionalised bipolar Europe and shaped every later crisis.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Cominform and Comecon
key_individuals_and_groups.relevance: Soviet political and economic instruments for controlling Eastern Europe in response to Marshall aid and Western unity.

gaps.note: This option is a wider world depth study (Paper 1 Section B), not a British depth study, so no specified historic environment site applies. Field set to null per schema.

Spec does not require named historians at GCSE. Lessons reference disagreement about Cold War origins generically (orthodox vs revisionist framing) without naming Gaddis or Westad in student-facing content, per the brief's guidance to use historiography only if examiner reports flag it.

Spec ends at 1972 with SALT 1; the breakdown of Détente in the late 1970s and the second Cold War of the 1980s sit outside this option. Lesson 14 flags the misconception that Détente equals the end of the Cold War without teaching post-1972 events.
